newsitem.title: GERMANY: SPD's Scharping talks tough before Kohl tax summit.
newsitem.headline: SPD's Scharping talks tough before Kohl tax summit.

text.p: Opposition Social Democrats (SPD) hardened their rhetoric early on Monday before a "tax summit" between Chancellor Helmut Kohl and SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine aimed at early implementation of tax reform.

SPD parliamentary faction leader Rudolf Scharping said in a television interview the reform must benefit normal wage earners and those who are really contributing to the economy, by cutting non-wage costs.

"We are obligated to help the nation, not the government. That we don't want. (We want to) create order, lessen the burdens on citizens, to revive the economy but not to perfume a pile of manure," Scharping told a ZDF interviewer.
He said his party would not make concessions on tax breaks for those who work unsocial hours, the elimination of which is a key part of Finance Minister Theo Waigel's reform plan.

"Over seven million people regularly work on Sundays, holiday and nights. We expect that they keep machinery working longer hours and that they apply their labour flexibly and intelligently. We don't want to penalise them retroactively," he said.
The unusual meeting between Kohl and Lafontaine, scheduled to start at 1400 GMT, is seen as a round of high-stakes poker aimed at the 1998 elections and the start of European monetary union in 1999.
The government needs SPD cooperation to pass its tax plans since the opposition controls the upper house of parliament.
In a separate radio interview, Scharping said Waigel's plans would tear a 50-billion mark ($29.9 billion) hole in the budget.
"In a nation with 4.7 million unemployed, we cannot afford to waste time or be unclear about the issues," he said.
Scharping said the SPD would also not tolerate cuts in pensions or life insurance. Nor would it accept a rise in the value-added tax to finance a cut in the top income tax rate.

Scharping saw room for agreement on the government's plan to cut the lowest tax rate. But reductions in the top rate should be subject to discussion of what tax breaks and subsidies were being eliminated, he said.
"(The reform) must benefit the maximum number of people who now consume their entire income and still don't have enough," he said.
Scharping said it was "really obscene...that the government wants to collect more from workers, while large private fortunes are made tax-free."
The SPD wants the government to implement its tax reform plan in January 1998, instead of a year later as Waigel plans.
-- Terence Gallagher, Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097150 ($ = 1.672 German Marks)
